newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Traders laud Tel Aviv's new stock-trading system.
newsitem.headline: Traders laud Tel Aviv's new stock-trading system.

text.p: Traders hailed on Thursday the advent of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's (TASE) "little bang" -- a continuous, order-driven trading system launched for dealings in a limited number of stocks.

"It will increase volume in the market, it will increase the efficiency of the market and it will increase the ability of big investors -- and foreign investors -- to act," said Eli Nahum, head of trading at Zannex Securities.
"I think it's fantastic," he said at the end of the first day of trading with the system.
Exchange officials and traders said they expect the Tel Aviv Continuous Trading (TACT) system to level the playing field for investors and boost turnover.

The centrepiece of TACT is the continuous trading session that runs from 10:00 a.m. until 3:30 p.m. Sunday through Thursday, the TASE's trading week. Traders can place orders at any time in any of the 10 securities participating in the first phase of TACT.
The exchange's computers are linked to the trading rooms of all the member brokerages and from there to their local branches, a network that delayed TACT's debut several times.
"You buy something and within two seconds you have the order done and within five seconds you have it confirmed," said one trader. "You know what you're doing."

TACT will gradually replace the TASE's "semi-continuous" system in which three securities at a time are traded in rounds. The old system made it difficult to fulfil trading orders, since there was only a limited number of rounds per day and long gaps between rounds.
Only the brokers themselves know between rounds what the supply/demand situation is. With TACT, orders are transferred immediately to the bourse and available for all traders to see and act on.
"There's no black curtain," said Jonathan Ross, vice president at Nesuah Securities.

Ester Levanon, the TASE's vice president for computers and operations, said the system would make it harder to manipulate share prices. "All the trading is uniform and a lot more fair. It's much more transparent."

Continuous trading is being accompanied by a package of smaller reforms. Orders and price changes of TACT-traded shares are now reported in agorot (one-hundredths of a shekel) rather than as a percentage.
Shares can no longer be tagged "buyers only" or "sellers only" and suspended from normal trading, and there are no limits on price fluctuations.

Traders said foreign investors -- who poured $500 million into Tel Aviv-traded shares in the first half of the year, up from $340 million in all of 1996 -- should be among the biggest beneficiaries of continuous trading.
"It's much more similar to a market they recognise," said Ross.

But more importantly, he said, continuous trading should increase liquidity by increasing trading opportunities. This will make it easier for big overseas institutions to move in and out of positions.

"When a foreigner goes into a stock, he takes a good look at his exit strategy," Ross said. At the moment, Ross estimates only about 30 to 40 of the more than 650 securities stocks traded on the TASE are sufficiently liquid.
In Thursday's trading, Formula Systems, one of 10 TACT shares, was among the top three most active shares, a fact brokers attributed to continuous trading.

Levanon said the TASE plans to gradually add new securities to TACT in blocs of 10, the next group joining in about three to four weeks. By the end of the year, she said, all the top 100 shares comprising the Mishtanim index would join TACT, including the top 25 shares of the Maof blue chip index.
She said continuous trading in bonds would be introduced in 1998.
But Nahum said he expected the TASE to speed up its schedule because continuous trading was so clearly better. "There will be pressure on the bourse to expand the system," he said.
